text:
Unofficial English Translation

Michaud
c. Bissonnette

2006 QCCA 775

COURT OF APPEAL

CANADA

PROVINCE OF QUEBEC

QUÉBEC

REGISTRY

No.

200-09-005100-059

(200-17-004014-031)

DATE:

June 8, 2006

CORAM:

THE HONOURABLE

JEAN-LOUIS BAUDOUIN
J.A.

LOUIS ROCHETTE J.A.

JULIE DUTIL J.A.

YVES MICHAUD

APPELLANT - plaintiff

v.

MICHEL BISSONNETTE,
in his capacity as President of the
National Assembly of
Quebec

RESPONDENT - defendant

JUDGMENT

[
1
]

THE COURT; - Ruling on the appeal from
a January 13, 2005 judgment of the Superior Court (the Honourable Jean
Bouchard) dismissing the appellant's motion for declaratory judgment;

[
2
]

Having examined the record, heard the parties
and taken the case under advisement;

[
3
]

For the reasons given by Dutil and Baudouin
JJ.A., with which Rochette J.A. concurs;

[
4
]

DISMISSES the appeal, without costs.

(s)

JEAN-LOUIS BAUDOUIN J.A.

(s)

LOUIS
ROCHETTE J.A.

(s)

JULIE
DUTIL J.A.

Mtre. André Bois

Mtre. Stéphane Rochette

Tremblay, Bois,
Mignault, Lemay

For the appellant

Mtre.
Raynold Langlois

Mtre.
François LeBel

Langlois, Kronström,
Desjardins

For the respondent

Date of hearing:

February 20, 2006

REASONS OF DUTIL J.A.

[
5
]

This appeal deals primarily with the scope of
the parliamentary privilege of free speech and of
section 21
of the
Charter
of human rights and freedoms
[1]

(the Charter).

THE FACTUAL CONTEXT

[
6
]

In June 2000, the Québec government created the
Commission des États généraux sur la situation et l'avenir de la langue
française au Québec (the Commission). The Commission
was mandated to prepare and submit to the Minister responsible for the Charter
of the French Language a report on the trends, priorities and consensuses
regarding the use, status and quality of the French language in Québec. The
Commission was also asked to make recommendations.

[
7
]

The Commission called public hearings to ensure
comprehensive thinking on the subject. The appellant's turn to speak during the
hearings came on December 13, 2000.

[
8
]

On December 11, 2000, two days prior to his
appearance before the Commission, the appellant made controversial remarks
about the Jewish people on a Montréal radio show.
The
Canadian Press
reported the incident as follows:
[2]

[TRANSLATION]

He said on the air that he told a
Jewish friend a month ago he was prepared to wait a hundred years for Québec
independence. His friend replied that Quebecers were not in the same situation
as the Jews before the creation of the State of Israel.

"The Armenians didn't suffer", Mr. Michaud
shot back at his friend. "The Palestinians aren't suffering. The Rwandans
aren't suffering. It's always you people. You're the only people in the world
who have suffered in human history".

[
9
]

When he appeared before the Commission on December 13, 2000, the appellant spoke about the
francization of immigrants. Acknowledging that a roughly 15-page address could
not be easily summarized in a few paragraphs, the judge in first instance
presented Mr. Michaud's remarks as follows:

[TRANSLATION]

[11] At the outset, the plaintiff
affirmed that over half of Québec immigrants are assimilated into the
English-speaking minority, which represents 8% of the Québec population. He
went on to say:

To
be or not to be assimilated?
That
is the question.
Québec
sovereignty is indispensable without the support, contribution and
determination of a substantial number of new Quebecers willing to journey with
us and play a role in building a society founded on social justice and freedom.

[12] Moving on to the failure of
the 1995 referendum, the plaintiff criticized as follows, for example, the
voting results in the Côte St-Luc Jewish community:

If
it were so [the francization of immigrants], we would not see results like the
1995 referendum results. I live on the edge of French-speaking and English-speaking
Montréal, in Côte St-Luc, where, as you can see in the appendix to this
document, there are 12 ridings, 2275 voters, not a single "yes" vote
in the 12 ridings. Not one "yes" vote, 2265
[
sic
]
"no votes". Not even a distracted student who voted "yes".
Not even a blind or visually impaired person who made a mistake.
It's zero intolerance.

. . .

.
. .
if immigrants, and the
ones in Côte St-Luc, they're a large proportion, understood us when we speak to
them, if they understood our language, if they understood the basic stakes for
a people entitled to their own homeland, maybe a few of them would vote
"yes", whereas it was a massive "no" vote.

[13] Here is what the plaintiff
said about those who advocate tolerance:

A
minority does not have to be tolerant. Tolerance is a virtue of the strongest,
of the Lord, it is a virtue of a master toward his slave. Masters are tolerant
of their slaves. Tolerance is for the strongest.

[14] Lastly, the plaintiff did
indeed refer to the Jewish people, but his comments were not the same as in his
radio interview beforehand:

My
fellow citizens should follow the example of Canon Groulx's remarks about the
Jewish people. Canon Groulx said and invited us, and I quote
"to have the Jews' fierce will to
survive, their indomitable spirit of solidarity, their indestructible moral
fibre".
The historian
then gave the example of the Jewish people as a model that Quebecers should
take to heart to affirm their own national identity and assume, fully assume,
the heritage of their history, adding that anti-Semitism was
"an un-Christian attitude and that,
spiritually, Christians are in a sense Semite". End of quote.

Canon
Groulx, who was a mentor of two (2) generations of Quebecers  and who had a
metro station named after him, which some people wanted renamed a few years
ago, no doubt to "Mordecai-Richler" station, boulevard René-Lévesque
no doubt to boulevard "Ariel Sharon", Place Jacques-Cartier probably
to Place "Galganov", and so forth. I'm being a bit satirical, I say
these things somewhat jokingly, but I think there are some who exaggerate and
push things a bit too far.

[
10
]

The next day, on December 14, 2000, Leader of
the Official Opposition Jean Charest asked Premier Lucien Bouchard during
question period in the National Assembly whether he agreed with the appellant's
remarks and would accept the appellant as his party's nomination candidate in
the riding of Mercier. In the preamble to his question, Mr. Charest summarized
the appellant's controversial remarks before the Commission:
[3]

[TRANSLATION]

And, to briefly recapitulate what
he said before the Commission yesterday, he talked about the ethnic vote
against the sovereignty of the Québec people, words that still resonate today
after the statements made by former premier Parizeau. He even added
"extremist", referring to B'nai Brith, he called it an anti-Québec,
anti-sovereigntist extremist movement.

[
11
]

Premier Bouchard replied immediately that he
rejected the appellant's remarks:
[4]

[TRANSLATION]

. . . I
therefore do not hesitate to say, on behalf of my party, on behalf of the
government, MNAs and all Quebecers, that we reject those remarks.

[
12
]

Mr. Charest then indicated that a motion
without notice would be moved that very day by an Opposition MNA and seconded
by another MNA:
[5]

[TRANSLATION]

That the National Assembly
uncompromisingly, unequivocally and unanimously denounces the unacceptable
remarks about ethnic communities and, in particular, the Jewish community, made
by Yves Michaud in Montréal, on December 13, 2000, at the Estates-General hearings on the French language.

[
13
]

The transcript of the appellant's remarks before
the Commission was not tabled. The motion having been presented by MNAs of the
party in power and the Opposition, there was no debate. However, a recorded
vote was held immediately and the 109 MNAs present voted in favour of carrying
the motion.

[
14
]

In the days that followed, the National
Assembly's motion fuelled public debate. Among other things, the appellant
received the support of some 30 sovereigntists, including former premier
Jacques Parizeau, who, in an open letter, denounced the motion carried by the
National Assembly. In their view, the motion was [TRANSLATION]
"a serious infringement of rights and freedoms and a flagrant act of
injustice".
[6]

[
15
]

The uproar over the affair continued until
January 11, 2001, when Premier Bouchard announced that he was leaving politics.
In his speech, he referred to the appellant's remarks, without naming him:
[7]

[TRANSLATION]

. . . "I still don't
understand", he said, "how the linguistic debate came to shift to a
comparative quantification of the suffering of the Jewish people and the
so-called intolerance shown by Quebecers who did not vote for Québec
sovereignty". He added that such statements harmed Québec's reputation
abroad.

[
16
]

The appellant responded to Mr. Bouchard in a
long letter dated December 31, 2000, which was published in the newspaper
La Presse
on
January 13, 2001.

[
17
]

On May 3, 2001, the appellant presented an initial petition to the National
Assembly. He asked to be heard by the Commission of the National Assembly in
order to enlighten its Members on the motion voted on December 14, 2000.

[
18
]

The petition was accepted and, around May 16, 2001, the appellant tabled a brief
setting forth his arguments for denouncing the adoption of the motion concerning
him. He asked that the National Assembly review its rules so [TRANSLATION] "that freedom of opinion and speech would never
again be censored".

[
19
]

The May 3, 2001 petition was never entered on
the Order Paper or debated. However, the appellant's brief is in the National
Assembly archives and may be consulted.

[
20
]

On December 13, 2001, the appellant presented
a new petition to the National Assembly. This time, he requested redress for
the injustice suffered. He proposed two remedies:

[TRANSLATION]

That the National Assembly
acknowledge that the vote on its motion of December 14, 2000 concerning the
remarks made by Yves Michaud was not preceded by the tabling of the transcript
of the remarks or by their full recitation in a plenary session and that,
accordingly, the MNAs could not judge the acceptability of the remarks before
supporting the motion.

OR

That the National Assembly declare
that, as an institution, it does not have the authority or power to express an
opinion endorsing or reproving remarks made by a citizen who is not one of its
Members.

[
21
]

In accordance with the
Standing Orders of the
National Assembly
(Standing Orders) in force at the time, petitions were to
be presented to the National Assembly and sent to Government House Leader
Jacques Brassard, and the government was to respond in writing within 60
days after the presentation of the petition. If the National Assembly was not
in session, the government had to respond in writing within three days after
the resumption of parliamentary proceedings.

[
22
]

On March 12, 2002, upon resumption of the
proceedings adjourned on December 21, 2001, Minister Jean-Pierre Charbonneau replied to the appellant,
informing him that, as Minister responsible for Parliamentary Reform, he would
be proposing as soon as possible [TRANSLATION] "a
new parliamentary provision on motions of censure against persons who are not
Members of the National Assembly".

[
23
]

According to an article published in the
newspaper
Le Devoir
on March 15, 2002, the appellant was satisfied with
the response. He stated that  [TRANSLATION] "this
puts an end to a painful episode in parliamentary history".

[
24
]

However, the 36th Legislature was dissolved on March 12, 2003, before the proposed amendment by
Minister Charbonneau was passed. The proposal thus lapsed.

[
25
]

On December 10, 2003, the appellant filed a
motion for declaratory judgment aimed essentially at having the following
declared:

[TRANSLATION]

The National Assembly does not have
constitutional authority to express, as a government institution or body, an
opinion endorsing or reproving remarks made by citizens who are not Members,
unless there is breach of the privileges recognized as necessary to carrying
out its legislative function.

The National Assembly did not have
the power to carry the motion of December 14, 2000 concerning the remarks
made by Yves Michaud.

The National Assembly is required
to rule on the petition presented by Yves Michaud on December 13, 2001 and
on any other petition that, for procedural reasons, the latter may have to
present to the National Assembly to obtain the redress for grievances called
for in the petition of December 13, 2001.

[
26
]

On January 13, 2005, the judge in first instance
dismissed the appellant's motion.

THE QUESTIONS IN DISPUTE

1.         DID THE NATIONAL ASSEMBLY OVERSTEP ITS POWERS
BY ADOPTING THE MOTION OF DECEMBER 14,
2000
?

The parties' arguments

[
27
]

The appellant called the privilege claimed by
the National Assembly [TRANSLATION] the "power to
rebuke or reprimand someone who is not a Member". He contended that, under
Standing Order 324, the National Assembly may exercise that power only if a
person is accused of breaching a parliamentary privilege.

[
28
]

Moreover, the appellant affirmed that the [TRANSLATION] "MNAs' privilege of freedom of speech" was not exercised when the National Assembly
adopted the resolution of December 14, 2000. He argued
that it is an individual rather than a collective privilege because it in fact
constitutes immunity for MNAs from all legal proceedings, be they civil or
penal, concerning acts related to their duties. It does not protect the acts of
the National Assembly as an institution.

[
29
]

The respondent argued that the National Assembly
exercised its privilege of freedom of speech in adopting the resolution of December 14, 2000. That privilege, and not what
the appellant called [TRANSLATION] "delivering a
rebuke or reprimand in the absence of any breach of a privilege", is held
by deliberative assemblies to ensure the proper functioning of parliamentary
institutions. The National Assembly would not be able to play its democratic
role without that privilege.

[
30
]

According to the respondent, the National
Assembly's authority to adopt resolutions in order to express its opinion is in
no way limited by Standing Order 324, since that procedure applies only to
individuals who breach the rights and privileges of the National Assembly or
its Members. In this case, the resolution of December 14, 2000 is a collective
manifestation of the opinion of the Members of the National Assembly in regard
to the appellant's remarks.

Analysis

[
31
]

The National Assembly, like the Canadian
Parliament and other legislative assemblies, holds certain privileges enabling
it to carry out its functions while ensuring compliance with the fundamental
principle of the constitutional separation of powers.

[
32
]

As the Supreme Court indicated in
Vaid
,
[8]

the preamble to the
Constitution Act, 1867
states the provinces'
intention to establish “a Constitution similar in Principle to that of the United Kingdom”. The principle of
parliamentary privilege was partially codified as of 1689 in the United Kingdom, in the
Bill of Rights
,
[9]

but the freedom of speech to which it refers was asserted at least as early as
1523.
[10]

[
33
]

Freedom of speech is recognized as a very
important inherent privilege necessary to an Assembly's ability to carry out
its functions and therefore protect democratic debate. In
New Brunswick
Broadcasting Co.
, the Supreme Court set forth the specific privileges that
arose in the United Kingdom:
[11]

Among the specific privileges which
arose in the
United
Kingdom
are the
following
:

(a)  freedom
of speech, including immunity from civil proceedings with respect to any matter
arising from the carrying out of the duties of a member of the House;

(b)  exclusive
control over the House's own proceedings;

(c)  ejection
of strangers from the House and its precincts; and

(d)  control
of publication of debates and proceedings in the House.

Erskine May,
supra
, provides convincing
justifications for each of these privileges:  see pp. 84, 90‑91,
171‑73, and 85‑86 respectively.
The need for the right of
freedom of speech is so obvious as to require no comment
.  . . .

[Emphasis
added.]

[
34
]

As pointed out by Binnie J. in
Vaid
,
parliamentary privileges are not, however, limitless. Not
everything that is done or said in an Assembly is necessarily tied to its
proceedings. When an Assembly or Member claims parliamentary privilege, the
sphere of activity for which privilege is claimed must be shown to be so
closely connected with the fulfilment of the Assembly's legislative and
deliberative functions that outside interference would undermine the autonomy
required by the Assembly and the member to do their work.
[12]

[
35
]

Freedom of speech is not a privilege held only
by individual Members, as contended by the appellant. It also protects motions
carried by the National Assembly, because they are opinions expressed
collectively by its Members. In Erskine May's
Treatise on The Law,
Privileges, Proceedings and Usage of Parliament
, "privilege" is
defined as follows:
[13]

Parliamentary privilege is the sum
of the peculiar rights enjoyed by each House collectively as a constituent part
of the High Court of Parliament, and by Members of each House individually,
without which they could not discharge their functions, and which exceed those
possessed by other bodies or individuals. Thus
privilege, though part of the law of the land, is to a certain extent an
exemption from the ordinary law.  . . .

. . . the privileges of Parliament
are rights which are “absolutely necessary for the due execution of its
powers”.  . . .

[
36
]

In Great Britain, a joint parliamentary
committee examined the privilege of free speech and section 9 of the
Bill of
Rights
of 1689. In its report, the committee affirmed that freedom of
speech is not a privilege held by individual members, but clearly the privilege
of the deliberative assembly as a whole:

. . . freedom of speech is the
privilege of the House as a whole and not of the individual member in his own
right, although an individual member can assert and rely on it.

[
37
]

This privilege does not serve solely to provide
MNAs with immunity from civil or penal proceedings, as affirmed by the
appellant. Rather, their immunity is a component of
parliamentary privilege. Professors Henri Brun and Guy
Tremblay wrote the following in this regard:
[14]

[TRANSLATION]

Members of legislative assemblies enjoy certain immunities
overriding general law that enable them to adequately carry out their
functions.
These individual immunities are part of a broader set of
exceptional rights held by Assemblies; they are "parliamentary
privileges", which we will study later on
.

[Emphasis
added.]

[
38
]

The British joint committee was also of the
opinion that parliamentary privilege is comprised of rights and immunities held
by Parliament and its members:
[15]

3. Parliamentary privilege consists
of the rights and immunities which the two Houses of Parliament and their
members and officers possess to enable them to carry out their parliamentary
functions effectively.  . . .

[
39
]

In the present case, in unanimously adopting a
motion denouncing the appellant's remarks, the MNAs expressed an opinion
different from the appellant's. Standing Orders 185 and 186 state the goals and
objectives of motions carried by the National Assembly:

185. Matter submitted to
Assembly for decision
― A Member who wishes to obtain the decision of the Assembly on some
matter shall make a motion for that purpose.

186. Orders and resolutions
― Every motion, when carried, becomes
either an order or a resolution of the Assembly. By its orders the Assembly directs
its committees, its Members, or any other person to do something;
by its
resolutions the Assembly declares its own opinions and purposes or affirms some
fact
or principle.

An order
or a resolution may be discharged or rescinded only upon motion by a minister
to that effect, which motion shall not require notice
.

[Emphasis
added.]

[
40
]

Once a motion expressing an opinion is adopted,
it becomes a resolution.

[
41
]

Such a resolution is very different from a law
voted by the National Assembly, in that it is protected by the privilege of
freedom of speech. Contrary to a law, a resolution is merely a means of
expressing an opinion of the MNAs and has no normative effect.

[
42
]

The appellant's argument that Standing Order 324
limits the National Assembly's power to reprimand a person other than an MNA
cannot be accepted. The Standing Order reads as follows:

324. Question of privilege and
notice of motion
― Any Member who believes that a person who is not a Member of
Parliament has breached the privileges of the Assembly or one of its members
may move a motion impugning his conduct.

The Member so complaining
shall first raise a question of privilege and then announce that he intends to
move a motion respecting the matter.

[
43
]

In my opinion, as contended by the respondent,
this Standing Order in no way curtails the parliamentary privilege of freedom
of speech, which is vast and allows an Assembly and its Members to express a
diverging opinion on a current political issue. The objective of the Standing
Order is entirely different. It establishes the applicable procedure when an
MNA, by means of a motion, impugns the conduct of a person other than an MNA, who
is said to have breached the rights or privileges of the Assembly or one of its
Members. That is not the case here. The National Assembly and its Members can
express an opinion by adopting a resolution without following the procedure set
forth in Standing Order 324.

[
44
]

The appellant also argued that the National
Assembly cannot invoke the privilege of freedom of speech in the circumstances
of this case since, by adopting the resolution of December 14, 2000, it was not
acting within the bounds of its legislative or executive supervision functions.

[
45
]

The judge in first instance rightly dismissed
that argument:

[TRANSLATION]

[49] The Court is far from
convinced that the National Assembly, given the central position it occupies in
our system of government, is prohibited from denouncing remarks that its
Members collectively find unacceptable. While it is true that the principal
mission of the National Assembly is to study and pass bills, as well as to
supervise government activity, the Court does not believe that its powers are
restricted to that role.

[50] Even an inattentive observer
of the parliamentary scene cannot help but note the wide range of issues
discussed during the sittings of the National Assembly, independently of the
tabling of bills and the examination of government acts (Standing Orders
51-54). Were MNAs or the National Assembly to be questioned outside this very
limited framework without the possibility of invoking parliamentary privilege,
the very functioning of this forum, where a great diversity of ideas collide
and which represents [TRANSLATION] "a  microcosm
of Québec society with its complexity and variety", could be called into
question (Jean-Noël Lavoie,
Organisation et
fonctionnement de l'Assemblée nationale
, Québec, 1976 at 5).

[
46
]

The joint committee of the British Parliament
affirmed that freedom of speech is the single most important parliamentary
privilege. Among other things, it protects one of the primary functions of
Parliament, namely, that of debating and passing resolutions freely on the
subjects of its own choosing:
[16]

36. A primary function of
Parliament is to debate and pass resolutions freely on subjects of its own
choosing. This is a cornerstone of parliamentary democracy. The performance of
this function is secured by the members of each House having the right to say
what they will (freedom of speech) and discuss what they will (freedom of
debate). These freedoms, the single most important parliamentary privilege, are
enshrined in article 9 of the Bill of Rights 1689. Using modern spelling,
article 9 provided:

That
the freedom of speech and debates or proceedings in Parliament ought not to be
impeached or questioned in any court or place out of Parliament.

In this article the meaning of
"impeach" is not clear: possible meanings include hinder, challenge
and censure.

[
47
]

Thus, the National Assembly exercises not only
legislative and supervision functions, but also the functions of a deliberative
assembly.

[
48
]

In this case, the Members of the National
Assembly collectively expressed an opinion denouncing the remarks made by the
appellant in conjunction with a commission set up by the government [TRANSLATION] "to study the situation and future of the French
language in Québec". The National Assembly
expressed itself in a unanimous resolution on a current political issue
in Québec. The appellant freely chose to take part in the public debate.
The National Assembly therefore acted within its purview.

[
49
]

In conclusion, both the National Assembly and
its Members exercised the privilege of freedom of speech by carrying, on
December 14, 2000, the motion denouncing the remarks made by the appellant in
his appearance before the Commission on December 13, 2000.

The role of the courts

[
50
]

The role of the courts is limited when
parliamentary privilege is invoked. Courts can verify only its existence and
extent, not its exercise. McLachlin J. stated the following in
New Brunswick
Broadcasting Co.
:
[17]

The
general rule which has developed from the above and subsequent case law is that
courts will inquire into the existence and extent of privilege, but not its
exercise
. . . .

[
51
]

Consequently, the judge in first instance
rightly concluded that he did not have jurisdiction to examine the merits of
the motion. It is not up to the courts to judge a motion's timeliness, soundness
or appropriateness.

2.
DOES SECTION 21 OF
THE CHARTER ALLOW THE COURTS TO REVIEW THE NATIONAL ASSEMBLY'S RULING ON A
PETITION TABLED BY A MEMBER OF THE PUBLIC?

[
52
]

The judge in first instance concluded that the
Superior Court could not compel the National Assembly, under
section 21
of the

Charter
, to rule on a petition; its action on a petition comes under the
National Assembly's inherent privilege of controlling its own proceedings.

[
53
]

The appellant argued that petitioning was a
favour before the passage of the
Charter
in 1975. It became a new right of a
quasi-constitutional nature when it was enshrined in the Charter, in
section
21
. That section now has normative value and must be applied.

[
54
]

The respondent contended that the passage of

section 21
of the
Charter
did not repeal the National Assembly's privilege of
controlling its proceedings without outside interference.

[
55
]

In my view,
section 21
of the
Charter
does not
have the scope conferred on it by the appellant.
Section
21
reads as follows:

21.
Every person has a right of petition to the National
Assembly for the redress of grievances
.

[
56
]

A number of authors quoted by the judge in first
instance define a petition as an official request to an authority to obtain the
redress of some wrong:

Raymond Guillien and Jean Vincent,
Lexique
des termes juridiques
, Dalloz, 13th ed., 2001:

[TRANSLATION]

Petition (constitutional law).
A non-contentious proceeding that a member of the public may address
in writing to parliamentary assemblies to denounce abuse by an administration,
advocate a legislative amendment, etc. Proceeding seldom used today.

Joseph R. Nolan and Jacqueline M.
Nolan-Haley,
Black's Law Dictionary
, 6th ed. (The Publisher's Editorial Staff, 1990):

[IN ENGLISH]

Petition.
A written address, embodying an application or prayer from the
person or persons preferring it, to the power, body, or person to whom it is
presented, for the exercise of his or their authority
in the redress of some
wrong,
or the grant of some favor, privilege, or license. A formal written
request addressed to some governmental authority. The right of the people to
petition for redress of grievances is guaranteed by the First Amendment, U.S.
Constitution.

John A. Yogis,
Canadian Law
Dictionary
, 2nd ed.,
Barron's Educational Series, Inc.:

Petition.
A prayer (formal request) from a person or group to a power or
person for the exercise of his authority
in the redress of some wrong.

In old English law, a petition was addressed to the King and later to the
Chancellor in a situation where a case was beyond the ordinary writ system. In
present day, a divorce proceeding is started by petitioning the court.

Robert Marleau and Camille
Montpetit,
House of Commons Procedure and Practice
, House of Commons,
Ottawa (Chenelière/McGraw–Hill: Montréal/Toronto):

Simply defined, a petition is a
formal request to an authority
for redress of a grievance
. Public
petitions, addressed to the House of Commons and presented to the House by its
Members, constitute one of the most direct means of communication between the people
and Parliament. Certainly, it is among the most ancient; the act of petitioning
has been described as “the oldest of Parliamentary forms", "the
fertile seed of all proceedings of the House of Commons”.

[
57
]

Contrary to the appellant's claims, the right of
petition is a very old right the exercise of which is subject to the privileges
of the National Assembly. The judge in first instance clearly summarized the
state of the right:

[TRANSLATION]

[62] In response to that argument,
it should be borne in mind that the right of citizens to address a petition to
parliament for redress of a grievance existed well before it was codified in
the
Charter
in 1975:

All authorities agree that
the right of petitioning parliament for redress of grievances is acknowledged
as a fundamental principle of the constitution. It has been uninterruptedly
exercised from very early times and has had a profound effect in determining
the main forms of parliamentary procedure. (Speaker Gaspard Fauteux,
Debates
,
June 18, 1947 at 4275, in Robert Marleau and Camille Montpetit,
House
of Commons Procedure and Practice
, House of Commons, Ottawa,
Chenelière/McGraw-Hill: Montréal /Toronto at 923).

[63] The exercise of this very old
right has always been subject to or delimited by the privileges of the National
Assembly.

[
58
]

Passage of section 21 of the
Charter
was not
debated at all by a parliamentary committee.
[18]
It merely
reiterates the historical principle and cannot breach the National Assembly's
inherent privilege enacted, moreover, in section 42 of the
Act respecting
the National Assembly
:
[19]

42.
The Assembly has the power to protect its proceedings against all
interference.

[
59
]

Thus, the advent of
section 21
of the
Charter

did not create a new right. Furthermore, without specific Charter language to
the contrary, the Charter cannot breach one of the inherent parliamentary
privileges that arose in the United Kingdom,
[20]
since these
privileges have constitutional status.

[
60
]

McLachlin J. stated the following in
New
Brunswick Broadcasting Co.

in this regard:
[21]

I cannot, however, follow my colleague
Cory J. in concluding that "the
Charter
should apply to the actions
of the legislative assembly" (p. 401), if he means by this that the
Charter

should apply to
all of
the actions of the legislative assembly.
Absent
specific
Charter
language to the contrary, the long history of curial
deference to the independence of the legislative body, and to the rights
necessary to the functioning of that body, cannot be lightly set aside
,
even conceding that our notions of what is permitted to government actors have
been significantly altered by the enactment and entrenchment of the
Charter
.
The legal reason why curial deference to the action of the House of Assembly
here in issue should be preserved is set out below
.

[Emphasis
added.]

[
61
]

Professors Brun and Tremblay
[22]

dealt specifically with the scope of
section 21
of the
Charter
. They concluded that the courts cannot ensure it is applied. Only the
National Assembly has that right:

[TRANSLATION]

. . . Similarly,
section 21 of the
Charter of human rights and freedoms
, R.S.Q., c. C-12,
which sets forth the right of all persons to petition the National Assembly,
may be applied only by the National Assembly itself: see orders 62
et seq.

of the
Standing Orders of the National Assembly
, and the October 24,
2000 decision of the President of the National Assembly in regard to the
petition Jacques Dubreuil sought to present.  . . .

. . . What we have seen in this
regard with respect to the
Canadian Charter
(in I.B.) is also true for the

Québec Charter
, so that, for example, it would be prohibited for the courts to
try to ensure the application of
section 21
of the
Charter
, under which all
persons may petition the National Assembly.

[
62
]

Thus, the judge in first instance rightly
refused to order the National Assembly to rule on the appellant's petition of
December 13, 2001, as that would have breached the Assembly's privilege to have
exclusive control over its debates.

CONCLUSION

[
63
]

I propose that the appeal be dismissed, but
without costs, given the nature of the dispute.

(s)

JULIE DUTIL J.A.

REASONS OF BAUDOUIN J.A.

[
64
]

I agree with the analysis and conclusions of my
colleague Dutil J.A. However, I cannot help but think that the Law in this case
presents a strange paradox.

[
65
]

To preserve parliamentary democracy and, hence,
the free flow of ideas, the Law at the time of the charters and the
predominance of individual rights means that an individual can be condemned for
his ideas (good or bad, politically correct or incorrect, it matters little) without
appeal and then publicly hung out to dry without having had a chance to defend
himself and even without the reasons for his condemnation having first been
clearly stated before his judges, the parliamentarians. "
Summum jus
summa injuria
", as the Roman jurists would have said!

(s)

JEAN-LOUIS BAUDOUIN J.A.
